links.outcome: Local discrimination and calibration of published PREVENT equations in Duke EHR data
links.effect: Discrimination strong (C-index 0.75-0.77 vs 0.76-0.79 in validation cohort), but risk was underestimated in the relaxed cohort, especially for Black, high-ADI, and Medicaid/uninsured patients.
links.quote: Calibration ratios were higher in the strict cohort, indicating greater underestimation of CVD risk in the broader relaxed cohort, especially among Black patients, those in more disadvantaged ADI quartiles, and those with Medicaid or no insurance (eFigure 8, eFigure 9, and eTable 2 in Supplement 1 ).

links.outcome: Effect of local retraining and recalibration on discrimination and calibration
links.effect: Local retraining and recalibration yielded similar C-indices; recalibration modestly improved calibration but risk remained underestimated for most subgroups.
links.quote: Recalibration modestly improved calibration, but risk remained underestimated for most subgroups, particularly Black patients, higher ADI quartiles, and those with Medicaid or no insurance (eFigure 12, eFigure 13, and eTable 4 in Supplement 1 ); decile-based calibration plots are shown in eFigure 14 and eFigure 15 in Supplement 1 .

links.outcome: Subgroup discrimination and calibration by race, ADI, and insurance
links.effect: C-index lowest in Black individuals, highest ADI quartile, and Medicare patients; calibration worse for disadvantaged subgroups.
links.quote: Asian males showed the highest C-index, and Black individuals showed the lowest.

links.outcome: Model performance across demographic and socioeconomic subgroups
links.effect: Discrimination declined with increasing neighborhood disadvantage; Black patients had lowest C-index in both Duke cohorts, unlike in PREVENT cohorts.
links.quote: Model performance declined with increasing neighborhood disadvantage, with the poorest discrimination in the highest ADI quartile.

links.outcome: Calibration under missing laboratory and vital sign data across subgroups
links.effect: Missingness was greater among underserved groups (TC missing 52.2%); calibration was worse in the relaxed cohort especially among disadvantaged subgroups.
links.quote: However, calibration was worse in the relaxed cohort, especially among disadvantaged subgroups (Black patients, higher ADI quartiles, and those with Medicaid or no insurance), suggesting missingness is associated with poorer calibration even when discrimination is preserved.

links.outcome: Differences between PREVENT development cohorts and local Duke population
links.effect: Duke cohorts were more racially diverse (Black 26.4% vs 9.1%), with higher CVD event rates (7.1% vs 2.9% in females) and smoking; performance differences followed.
links.quote: CVD events were more frequent in Duke data (17 023 females [7.1%] and 14 483 males [8.7%] in the relaxed cohort and 3910 females [5.5%] and 3700 males [6.6%] in the strict cohort) than in PREVENT derivation (53 258 females [2.9%] and 53 403 males [3.7%]) and validation (54 365 females [2.9%] and 50 489 males [3.5%]) cohorts, as were ASCVD and HF events.
